categories.intro: Code Patterns. How objects and modules come together. tools.blurb: Translate between an interface your code wants and one that an existing component provides.

tools.blurb: Put a simple front door on a complicated subsystem so callers don't pay for everything inside.

tools.blurb: Translate between bounded contexts so a foreign model can't quietly contaminate yours.

tools.blurb: Talk to the outside world through narrow interfaces (ports) implemented by swappable adapters.

tools.blurb: Hide persistence behind a collection-like interface so domain code can pretend storage doesn't exist.

tools.blurb: Persist the sequence of events that produced state instead of just the latest state.

tools.blurb: Write the event into the same transaction as the state change, then ship it from the table later.

tools.blurb: Coordinate a long-running transaction as a sequence of local steps with compensations instead of a global commit.

tools.blurb: Precompute the result of an expensive query and refresh it on a schedule or on demand.

categories.intro: Architecture Patterns. How services agree on what happened. Request/Response, Work Queues, Dead Letter Queues, Idempotency Keys, and Choreography vs. Orchestration are the wiring decisions behind any system that crosses a network and still needs to be reasoned about.
categories.name: Messaging & Coordination

tools.blurb: The synchronous backbone of distributed systems: send a message, block until the answer arrives.
tools.name: Request / Response

tools.blurb: Decouple producers from consumers with a queue and competing-consumer workers, so load and rate are separate.
tools.name: Work Queues

tools.blurb: Move messages that keep failing into a side queue so the main queue keeps draining and you can investigate later.
tools.name: Dead Letter Queue

tools.blurb: Let callers safely retry by tagging each attempt with a key the server uses to deduplicate effects.
tools.name: Idempotency Keys

tools.blurb: Decide whether services react to events on their own (choreography) or follow a conductor (orchestration).
tools.name: Choreography vs. Orchestration

categories.intro: Architecture Patterns. The shape of the deployment. Monolith, Microservices, Modular Monolith, Backends for Frontends, Strangler Fig boundary, Service Mesh, and Sidecar are about where the seams between teams and runtimes actually live.
categories.name: Topology

tools.blurb: One deployable for the whole system; the default that earns its critics only at certain sizes of team and traffic.
tools.name: Monolith

tools.blurb: Independently deployable services drawn around team boundaries, paid for with operational overhead.
tools.name: Microservices

tools.blurb: One deployable, hard module boundaries inside it: the alternative most teams should try before splitting.
tools.name: Modular Monolith

tools.blurb: A thin per-client backend that shapes APIs for one frontend instead of forcing one API to serve all.
tools.name: Backends for Frontends

tools.blurb: Wrap the old system behind a façade and grow the new one inside it until the old can be deleted.
tools.name: Strangler Fig (boundary tactic)

tools.blurb: Move retries, mTLS, and routing into a sidecar layer so application code stops re-implementing them per service.
tools.name: Service Mesh

tools.blurb: Run a helper process next to your service to add capabilities (proxying, telemetry) without changing the service.
tools.name: Sidecar

categories.intro: Architecture Patterns. How a system bends without breaking when things go sideways. Bulkhead between services, Circuit Breaker across services, Back-pressure, Load Shedding, and Graceful Degradation are the moves that turn partial failure into a user-acceptable outcome.
categories.name: Resilience at Scale

tools.blurb: Isolate workloads across deployments or pools so one tenant or workload can't sink the others.
tools.name: Bulkhead (service-level)

tools.blurb: Stop sending traffic to a downstream that's clearly hurting, then probe before declaring it healthy again.
tools.name: Circuit Breaker (between services)

tools.blurb: Tell upstream callers to slow down when you're full, instead of silently absorbing or dropping.
tools.name: Back-pressure

tools.blurb: Drop or reject low-priority work near capacity so the critical path stays inside its latency budget.
tools.name: Load Shedding

tools.blurb: Decide in advance what features get turned off when dependencies fail, so 'works' has a defined floor.
tools.name: Graceful Degradation

categories.intro: Architecture Patterns. How a system changes shape without stopping. Strangler Fig at the system level, Expand/Contract Schema, Parallel Run, Dark Launches, and Feature Flags as architecture are the patterns of taking a running system from one shape to a better one without an outage.
categories.name: Evolution & Migration

tools.blurb: Replace a legacy system incrementally by routing traffic to the new implementation feature by feature.
tools.name: Strangler Fig (system migration)

tools.blurb: Add the new shape, dual-write, migrate readers, then remove the old shape — never with all four at once.
tools.name: Expand / Contract Schema

tools.blurb: Run the old and new implementations side by side against real traffic until results agree, then switch.
tools.name: Parallel Run

tools.blurb: Ship the new code into production behind a flag and exercise it with real traffic before any user sees it.
tools.name: Dark Launches

tools.blurb: Use long-lived flags to keep architectural choices reversible, not just to gate user-visible features.
tools.name: Feature Flags (as architecture)

categories.intro: Patterns of Discipline. How big changes ship in small, reversible steps. Branch by Abstraction, Expand/Contract Schema+API, Parallel Change, and Feature Toggles are about keeping main shippable while a multi-week refactor or migration is in flight.
categories.name: Change Patterns

tools.blurb: Hide the thing being replaced behind an interface, swap implementations behind it, then collapse the seam.
tools.name: Branch by Abstraction

tools.blurb: A discipline for changing schemas and APIs without downtime: add the new shape, migrate, then remove the old.
tools.name: Expand / Contract (Schema & API)

tools.blurb: Make a breaking change in three steps — expand, migrate callers, contract — so the tree always compiles.
tools.name: Parallel Change

tools.blurb: Keep work-in-progress in main behind toggles, separating deploy from release and shortening branch lifetimes.
tools.name: Feature Toggles (as discipline)

categories.intro: Patterns of Discipline. How a team agrees the work is done. Review-as-Conversation, Characterization Tests, Golden/Snapshot tests, Property-Based Testing, and Mutation Testing are about raising the floor of trust without lengthening the queue.
categories.name: Review & Verification

tools.blurb: Treat review as the moment a second engineer understands the change, not as the moment correctness is decided.
tools.name: Review-as-Conversation vs. Review-as-Gate

tools.blurb: Pin down the actual behavior of legacy code with tests before you change anything, so a regression is detectable.
tools.name: Characterization Tests

tools.blurb: Record the current output as truth and fail when it changes, useful when the spec is 'whatever it does today.'
tools.name: Golden / Snapshot Tests

tools.blurb: State invariants and let the runner generate inputs to break them, instead of guessing the edge cases yourself.
tools.name: Property-Based Testing

tools.blurb: Modify the program in small ways and check that some test fails, measuring how much your suite actually catches.
tools.name: Mutation Testing

categories.intro: Patterns of Discipline. How a team keeps the running system trustworthy. Runbooks as Code, the Four Golden Signals, Error Budgets, Blameless Postmortems, and On-Call as Pattern are the small habits that compound into operational excellence.
categories.name: Operational Patterns

tools.blurb: Version, review, and execute runbooks alongside the code they describe, so they age with the system.
tools.name: Runbooks as Code

tools.blurb: Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation: the minimum monitoring vocabulary every service should publish.
tools.name: Four Golden Signals

tools.blurb: Turn 'how reliable' into a budget the team spends on changes versus burns on outages, with a written policy.
tools.name: Error Budgets

tools.blurb: Investigate incidents by asking how each action made sense to the operator in the moment, then fix the system.
tools.name: Blameless Postmortems

tools.blurb: Treat the rotation, alert quality, and follow-up as the artifact, not just the schedule of who's paged.
tools.name: On-Call as Pattern

categories.intro: Anti-Patterns. The shapes worth naming so you can refuse them. Each entry below is something that solved a real problem at first and then quietly went toxic. Recognizing the shape is the whole point — the cure is usually one of the patterns above.
categories.name: Anti-Patterns

tools.blurb: Microservices that must be deployed together: you've paid the cost of distribution and kept the coupling of a monolith.
tools.name: Distributed Monolith

tools.blurb: One class that knows everything and is touched by every change — the gravitational center the rest of the system orbits.
tools.name: God Object

tools.blurb: Modeling domain concepts with bare strings, ints, and dicts so the type system can't help catch a misuse.
tools.name: Primitive Obsession

tools.blurb: Domain objects with no behavior, just getters and setters, with business logic scattered across service classes instead.
tools.name: Anemic Domain Model

tools.blurb: Drawing service boundaries before you know the domain, locking in coupling that later proves expensive to move.
tools.name: Microservices Too Early

tools.blurb: Pulling out an interface before the second concrete case exists, freezing a guess as if it were a constraint.
tools.name: Premature Abstraction

tools.blurb: Deduplicating code that only looks alike, gluing unrelated concepts together so changes in one place break the other.
tools.name: DRY at All Costs

tools.blurb: A homegrown DSL in YAML or JSON that grows control flow until it's a language with no compiler, debugger, or tests.
tools.name: Configuration-Driven Development

tools.blurb: The system shape that emerges when no shape is enforced: tangled, unstructured, and somehow still in production.
tools.name: Big Ball of Mud

tools.blurb: Hidden shared mutable state dressed up as a design pattern, so dependencies stop showing up in signatures.
tools.name: Singleton-as-Global-State

tools.blurb: Encoding meaning into strings the compiler can't see, so misspellings and confusions only show up at runtime.
tools.name: Stringly-Typed Code

tools.blurb: Hooks, parameters, and indirection added for a case that never arrives, paid for in confusion by every reader since.
tools.name: Speculative Generality

faqs.answer: The honest version: read the catalog before you start, then ignore it while you write the obvious solution, then come back when the obvious solution starts to hurt. Patterns are most useful as names for a shape you've already drawn at least once — they shorten the next conversation about it, they don't replace the first attempt. Fowler's Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture is the best 'read once, refer back forever' starting place.
faqs.question: How do I choose a pattern instead of writing one from scratch?
faqs.source_label: Martin Fowler: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture

faqs.answer: When changing one service requires deploying others in lockstep, you're paying the operational cost of distribution and keeping the coupling of a monolith. The diagnostic: if every release ships more than one service, or if your release notes are organized by 'changes in services A, B, and C this week,' the seams are wrong. Fowler's MonolithFirst remains the cleanest argument for delaying the split until you've actually learned where the boundaries are.
faqs.question: When is a 'microservice' actually a distributed monolith in disguise?

faqs.answer: Expand and contract: add the new shape, dual-write to both, migrate readers, then remove the old. Each step is a deploy in its own right; you never do more than one shape-changing step at a time. The same dance applies to APIs (parallel change) and to system-level rewrites (strangler fig). Sadalage and Fowler's evolutionary database design essay is the reference, and Tim Evans' walkthrough is the cleanest working-engineer post on the discipline.
faqs.question: How do I migrate a schema without an outage?

faqs.answer: If you treat them as code with a lifecycle, yes; if you treat them as runtime configuration with no expiry, no. The flags that pay off are short-lived release toggles that come out within a release or two, and a small handful of long-lived ops toggles that you actually exercise. Pete Hodgson's reference taxonomy separates the four kinds and is the right place to start. The anti-pattern is a flag graveyard where nobody knows which branches are live in production.
faqs.question: Are feature flags worth the complexity they add?

faqs.answer: When you can state an invariant — a sentence of the form 'for any input that looks like X, the output must satisfy Y' — and the cost of finding the edge cases yourself is too high. PBT is especially good for parsers, serializers, and pure functions on domain types; less good when the function's behavior is irreducibly example-shaped. The Hypothesis project's intro essay is the working-engineer entry point, and Wlaschin's railway oriented programming pieces compose well with it.
faqs.question: When should I reach for property-based testing instead of examples?

faqs.answer: Because you're changing behavior without a harness, and you don't yet have a definition of what 'unchanged' means. The answer Michael Feathers gave twenty years ago still holds: characterize the current behavior with tests before you change anything, even when those tests pin down behavior nobody likes. Then change the system in seams the tests cover. The Working Effectively with Legacy Code chapters on characterization tests and seams are the canonical reference.
faqs.question: Why does refactoring legacy code keep producing regressions?

faqs.answer: When the cost of moving away from it exceeds the cost of anything else you'd do this quarter, and when each new feature is paying interest on the same structural debt. Anti-patterns rarely cause incidents; they cause slowdown that's invisible until you compare your delivery cadence to a peer team's. The Big Ball of Mud paper is the most honest description of how the shape arrives — by no decision, by every decision being local and time-pressured. The cure is always a sequence of small, named patterns above, applied with patience.
faqs.question: Where does an anti-pattern stop being a smell and start being a crisis?
faqs.source_label: Foote & Yoder: Big Ball of Mud
